note: The contract between the plugin and the resource pack. The plugin emits these codepoints; the pack draws them. Nothing here is a visual decision: it assigns identities and sizes, not appearances.

status.purpose: Status and stack icons shown beside a readout.

ability.purpose: Ability slots. Count follows the harness class inputs: A1, A2, ultimate.

panel.purpose: Background panel pieces for a bossbar title strip.

infrastructure.purpose: The four recognized forms plus the Level 6 alternative.

hunger.purpose: Hunger readout. The vanilla row is hidden by this pack because a static texture cannot tell an empty drumstick a player could refill from one their Capacity does not grant. Three states are therefore drawn here, plus a half step.

hidden_vanilla_sprites.purpose: Nothing is hidden any more. The hunger row used to be blanked so the plugin could draw a glyph readout that distinguished a refillable empty drumstick from one beyond the player's Capacity. Repainting the row as a bar makes it legible in its native position instead, and the Capacity question moves to a number in the sidebar.

placeholder_shapes.purpose: Which SHAPE a glyph gets. These distinguish STATES from one another so a readout is legible, and encode no palette, icon language or artwork. A glyph with no entry gets the default index-marked outline, which is deliberately identical everywhere so a wrong codepoint reads as a wrong icon.

vocabulary.half: filled on the left, outlined on the right
vocabulary.blank: nothing at all, but still occupying its width

placeholder_shapes.blank_note: 'blank' is not a placeholder. A state whose meaning is 'there is nothing here' renders as nothing, and that is the finished appearance rather than something waiting to be drawn. It keeps its advance so the row stays a fixed ten drumsticks wide and Capacity fills it from the left, exactly as the vanilla row behaves.

bar_segments.purpose: The native health and hunger rows, repainted as segments of a continuous bar. Each row is ten sprites drawn side by side, so a segment design tiles into a bar in the native HUD position with the native fill logic -- no plugin, no boss bar, no action bar, and nothing to fade or contend over.
bar_segments.geometry: Sprites are 9x9 and spaced 8px apart, so the ninth column must stay clear or adjacent segments overlap by a pixel and the bar shows seams. The food row is drawn RIGHT TO LEFT from the right edge, which is why its half segment fills the opposite side from the heart one.
bar_segments.unstyled_variants: poisoned, withered, frozen, absorbing and vehicle hearts keep their vanilla art. They will read as drumsticks-and-hearts among bars when they appear, which is a visible gap rather than a hidden one.

bars.purpose: Fixed-size vitals bars with a proportional internal fill, built by REPEATING one unit glyph rather than by enumerating one image per fill level.
bars.why_repetition: A bitmap glyph cannot be stretched -- it renders at its texture size -- so a bar that grows is a bar made of repeated units. The bar is always `fill_width` units wide and only how many are LIT changes, which makes the fixed size structural instead of a property 130 separate images have to agree on. Four glyphs replace a hundred and thirty.
bars.why_not_the_native_row: The client owns the native health and hunger rows and its fill quantum is the half-sprite, so twenty steps is the most those rows can ever show. Repainting them (see bar_segments) buys the LOOK of a continuous bar and none of the resolution.
bars.advance: Each unit is one lit pixel wide, so Minecraft advances it by two -- the glyph's bounding box plus the standard one pixel of spacing. Each emission is therefore followed by U+F001 from the negative-space font, which advances -1, for a net advance of exactly one pixel per unit. If that assumption is ever wrong the bar collapses to a sliver rather than drifting subtly, which is the failure mode to want.
bars.codepoints_are_explicit: These declare their own base instead of taking the next sequential index. The sequential glyphs above are assigned by iteration order while the plugin hard-codes the resulting characters, so inserting a glyph shifts every later one silently.
bars.colour: Drawn WHITE and uncoloured, per this pack's rule that it assigns identity and never palette. The plugin tints the lit and unlit runs separately at render time, which is what makes an unfilled unit read as unfilled.
bars.ticks: Reference marks at a fixed interval of DISPLAYED health, so the bar carries absolute magnitude and not only a fraction. Without them 1,000/1,000 and 3,200/3,200 are the same full bar, which erases the x100 scale the project adopted specifically to make damage legible. The bar stays fixed width and the ticks get denser as max health grows, which is the arrangement that keeps a low-Capacity player from being given a visibly shorter bar.
bars.why_128: At 100 displayed health per tick, Mole's Lv30 3,200 is 32 ticks. Across 64 units that is one tick every 2px, which is a tick touching its neighbour. 128 gives 4px and room to read one.
bars.placement: Tall canvas, lit rows in the bottom `foot`. ascent 73 puts the bar where vanilla draws the native health and hunger rows (~30-39 GUI pixels above the bottom), by the measured law ascent = y + 46 with the bar sitting 4 rows up inside its foot. The native rows are blanked in the same pack, so the glyph bars replace them in place rather than sitting somewhere new.
bars.fill_width_is_a_layout_choice: 128 is the resolution the ticks want; 81 is what fits exactly where the native row is. The plugin picks, and features.vitalsBar.layout records which. See VitalsBar.Style.
bars.ascents_note: One set of units per candidate ascent, because ascent belongs to a PROVIDER and a bar that can be nudged without rebuilding the pack needs every position emitted up front. The plugin picks with features.vitalsBar.ascent. The placement law was fitted to screenshot pixels and is not accurate enough to land a bar first time -- rather than keep re-measuring it, the answer is made cheap to search. stride is the codepoint gap between sets, comfortably clear of the six units each set uses.

hud_layers.purpose: Declared vertical positions for HUD glyphs drawn in a bossbar title. ascent and height are per-PROVIDER, never per-emission, so each distinct (y, scale) pair costs one provider entry -- which is why these are named layers rather than a number the plugin passes.
hud_layers.x_is_different: Horizontal placement is the negative-space font and varies freely per emission. Only the vertical is enumerated. The asymmetry is the design, not a limitation of this table.
hud_layers.baseline_drift: Each bossbar is its own line with its own baseline and they stack downward, so the same ascent lands in a different place depending on WHICH bossbar drew it. Nominate one canvas bossbar and these values mean one thing.
hud_layers.fixtures: [BALANCE FIXTURE -- expect to tune] Every ascent below is a guess. Step one of docs/design/HUD_LAYER.md is measuring them against a real client with the probe glyph; nothing should be designed around these numbers until it has.
hud_layers.measured_27_september_2026: MEASURED against a real client, height 256, marks in the bottom 32 rows. Two rounds. The first, from verbal placement, fixed the SLOPE: one ascent unit is one GUI pixel, and the screen is about 256 GUI pixels tall. The second, from screenshots, fixed the INTERCEPT, which the first had wrong by twenty pixels: asc048 put its baseline at the very bottom of the hotbar, asc072 landed on the XP bar, asc128 about a third of the way up.
hud_layers.height_buys_reach: ascent cannot exceed height, and height SCALES the texture, so a high glyph must be declared tall AND drawn only in the bottom rows of a tall transparent canvas. That is the shape every real element needs, not a probe trick.
hud_layers.placing_something: ascent = desired_height_above_screen_bottom + 26, for height 256. A different height moves the whole line, since the foot sits (height - ascent) below the baseline -- so keep 256 unless there is a reason not to.

intended_use.asc008: off the bottom of the screen -- kept as the negative control
intended_use.asc048: baseline at the very bottom of the hotbar. MEASURED
intended_use.asc050: two pixels higher; kept only as a near neighbour of asc048
intended_use.asc080: clear of the XP bar: where the vitals bars belong
intended_use.asc092: above the ability row: the ability-refusal line
intended_use.asc128: about a third of the way up, beside the player. MEASURED

hud_layers.the_law: The foot of a height-256 glyph lands at (ascent - 46) GUI pixels above the bottom of the screen. So ascent = height_wanted + 46. The 46 is the bossbar baseline's own offset and is the part that had to be measured; the 1:1 slope could be reasoned about, and was.

bossbar_sprites.purpose: Blank the bossbar graphic so only the title renders. Once the bar is gone the bossbar stops being a bar and becomes a line of text we own, which is the whole technique.
bossbar_sprites.geometry: Vanilla bossbar sprites are 182x5. Replacing them with fully transparent images of the same size removes the bar without disturbing layout.
bossbar_sprites.why_keep_one: Something will eventually want a real progress bar. Blanking all seven colours is annoying to reverse for no gain, so PURPLE is left alone -- no current caller uses it.

hide_native_rows_note: Blank vanilla's health and hunger rows. Once the glyph bars draw INTO the slot those rows occupy, this stops being optional: a visible native row would sit underneath the replacement. It lives here rather than as a command-line flag because publish.py called build() with the default and so never hid anything, whatever the plugin config said. features.vitalsBar.hideNativeRows must agree, and a test binds them.
